The idea of a human or human-like being sort of subliming into a higher cognitive and often physical state is a venerable one in sci-fi, and is often a metaphor for human progress and potential. (Childhood's End is the most explicit instance of this, IMO, but in film, think the ending of 2001.) One way to understand the ending is as a very small-scale, personal, intimate use of the trope. Human progress here would be Theo getting unstuck. Often in a relationship where one partner is much older, the younger partner simply outgrows it. As you said:

>Samantha gets to experience real growth, love, and the emotions that come with it, and Theodore gets to revisit this experience from a more mature perspective, while also vicariously feeling them again.

So Samantha has this new experience. Now what? Does she stop there? Why would she or should she? Does the path forward into learning and growing more look like staying with someone who is, for understandable reasons of his own, going through a bit of a regression period and finding himself again? Often it doesn't. In a case like this one where the older partner is with the younger partly in order to look back or start over, that's simply not the younger partner's trajectory. The intersection of their two paths won't always last very long. Samantha's growing past the relationship is a departure, but it's also an invitation of sorts: the relationship with Samantha may have helped Theodore move on, but doesn't ultimately solve his problem - it's just a step. Like being with him was a step for her. They both need to grow past this point. Samantha does it; will he? The last shot of him and his friend whose AI companion has also left looking at the sunset seems to obviously pose this question. 

The fact that it's specifically a sunset (not sunrise, a new beginning, or just a view) adds some significant tension to that question. That trope I mentioned up top comes with a certain amount of fear. The new, more transcendent state of being is an unknown. What if that becoming makes us no longer human? Do we *want* to change that much? And yet if we don't, are we left behind in a terrible and irrevocable way? Is that a failure? This fear is often projected into representatives of the future, which are typically children or AI/cyborgs/robots. What will they be? Will it be bad? Will we recognize it at all?

I don't think it's too hard to see how this kind of anxiety can be worked into a human/AI relationship that is also a metaphor for a May/December relationship from the perspective of a man who is having a hard time moving forward. How much is he willing to change? How scary would it be not to? And to what degree is this backward-looking relationship (on his side) helping him change or helping him avoid it? The younger woman in this scenario is often a prop as much or more than a person. (I didn't say always, I said often.) The older man is going through something and she is a means of getting through it;  her whole being is often unconsciously overlooked. Samantha being an AI assistant is a pretty literal portrayal of that scenario. Samantha having many other human partners is an easy metaphor for the discovery that the younger woman who may have genuinely helped Theodore through a difficult period has an independent existence far beyond him that doesn't revolve around him. She wasn't there *to* fix him or support him; she was there, she did things that had that effect, and now she's moving on along her own trajectory that began before she met him and will continue afterward. "I can't live in your book anymore," i.e., I will not be continuing in the role I've been playing in your story; I can't continue to fill the position of someone in *your* story rather than following my own. Her outgrowing this role confronts him, again, with the question of his own growth, or lack thereof. This is just the scarier side of the coin (from his perspective), underlined by the fact that what she's growing into is beyond his comprehension.

Hey filmmakers!

I completed a 40-second gym promo called *Welcome to Fitbase*, and I wanted to share an insight about the process behind it. When researching gym videos, I noticed they all relied heavily on pumping music tracks to set the energy and pace of the edit. This got me thinking—what if I inverted that?

Instead of using music to drive the intensity, we recorded live sound on the day—everything from grunting and weights smashing to sweat dripping and feet pounding. These raw gym sounds became the percussive force behind the entire edit, building speed and tension until a (literally) breathless finish. No music, just pure gym atmosphere. It was a fun challenge, and it really made me think differently about how sound can shape a video.

My question for you all: Have you ever tried using only natural sound to create rhythm and pace in an edit, especially in something high-intensity like this? Do you think this approach works, or do audiences still expect that classic pump-up soundtrack for gym promos? I'd love to hear your thoughts on how this approach could be refined or applied to other projects!

Would be great to get your feedback on the video itself too—does it work without music, or does something feel missing?

Looking forward to your insights!

Cheers,  
Aaron

I see that you dismiss it as "cheesy" — and fair enough, though "cheesy" is not particularly useful criticism — but the last line of the movie — the revelation that the entire movie has been building to — is that Oppenheimer realizes too late that developing the atomic bomb has doomed the world. He has personally morally damned himself, which explains a lot of his behavior throughout the rest of the movie, especially after the bomb. 

Oppenheimer as shown in the movie is a man who thought he was doing something morally neutral, perhaps even morally good — creating a bomb that he believed would be created anyway, and doing it to defeat the Nazis. As it turned out, the bomb wasn't necessary to defeat the Nazis, the Nazis weren't close to creating a bomb themselves, and Oppenheimer saw that the moral calculations about using the bomb were simplistic at best. 

*Oppenheimer* takes as a given that creating the bomb was not a good thing, and is more interested in exploring why that particular man decided to take on that job, and how it affected him. I can understand people who think it lets him off the hook, or don't like Nolan's methods, but it's not a movie "about" the bomb, partly because I don't see anything in it that argues in the slightest that the bomb was worth it.

There's nothing wrong with reading film history, theory, or criticism and not caring if you find out things that might have surprised you. Part of being familiar with any art form is finding out what kinds of things become "common knowledge."

Is it nice to go in completely blind? Sure! If I was talking to someone who knew nothing about it, I'd avoid revealing much and encourage them to check it out without learning much more. All of this to say: If spoilers don't bother you, there's no reason to try to make them bother you. Read the books. I will always lean towards authorial intent over death of the author. In the same way that an axiom derived from science can only be 99 percent true as opposed to 100 percent true, there is still evidence to support it being a justified true belief epistemically which can be applied to a text. So to can we say from evidence present in text that there is a meaning to be derived inherent within it. We may not be able to say with a hundred percent certainty whether Banshees of Inishirin is an allegory for the Irish civil war, but we can say based on evidence that there is a stronger case that is than it is not and that we do so by seeing the evidence for what it is as a justified true belief. To say that Banshees of Inishirin is about what cats believe about Stalin, has no basis in evidence but under the view of death of the author would be equally as valid as the belief that the story is an allegory for the Irish civil war. One is a justified true belief, and the other is not. 

Personally, I’m not a fan of Barthes. His theory lends itself to nihilism more than existentialism. It’s not that there is no meaning to communicate, it is just that it is the author who imbues meaning whereas if we place the meaning as purely coming from the reader’s interpretation we reach a place where meaning has well, lost all meaning. Meaning from a linguistically semantic sense must be static. If say the word grass can mean anything in the whole dictionary as opposed to the specific static definition of vegetation consisting of typically short plants with long, narrow leaves, growing wild then the word has lost all meaning. Ultimately, applying the same logic, death of the author loses all meaning by placing meaning as any and everything a reader might conjecture thus losing meaning itself since meaning to some degree must be static. Thus Barthes and death of the author is ultimately nihilistic, not existential as many proponents would have us believe.

Why would a review specify that Anatomy of a Fall is *just* a courtroom drama? It’s very obviously not just that. The film uses the genre as a tool for exploring the inherent ambiguity of our subjectivity. A courtroom drama is a good tool for this because the task of a trial is the finding of fact, and courtroom dramas (and most movies) typically present a series of events as objective events in the story universe. Anatomy of a fall this turns the genre on its head to make a point about human subjectivity. 

Setting that aside for a moment, films can be exemplars of their respective genre - a great detective story, a great noir, a great thriller, a great comedy, a great horror story, a great court room drama, and so on. But films can do more than just tell good stories using accepted narrative and technical norms. Films can provide the audience with a transcendent experience that forces them to engage in critical reflection about the human experience. This is what great art does. I think Anatomy of a Fall is this kind of movie. It’s not *just* a genre movie. It’s not *just* telling a story. It is a deeply philosophical movie about the limits of our understanding. And it cleverly plays with genre tropes to do this. I think it was really brilliant in a way that most courtroom dramas aren’t.

To quote Ebert (again), the OP is confusing the inventory with the analysis. To say that there is depressing elements in a movie is not saying anything about what a movie ultimately does for the viewer. The OP stated that watching others "suffer" on screen is depressing, and others have responded that it is a form of catharsis. That is true; however, the real impact of a movie isn't just represented by the events included, but rather how the story in the end makes you feel. In the case of a good movie with depressing elements, by the end you always gain a sense of uplifting optimism or enlightenment. That's the benefit of watching good movies of *any* kind, not just those dealing with depressing subjects. Is Schindler's List depressing? I'd say not at all. I'd say something like Uwe Boll's Auschwitz, which also deals with the Holocaust, is a much more depressing movie, not because it is about the Holocaust, but rather because it's so terribly made. Along the same line, a movie that deals with uplifting subject matters don't always give you a boost - I still remember to this day how utterly depressed I felt after watching Bride Wars, a movie about weddings.

So in the end, we are not discussing what the movie *contains*, we must delve deeper and discuss what we as individuals get out of the movie. If, from watching excellent movies that deal with depressing subjects, all you get is a feeling of depression, then I suspect film is just not an art form suitable for you.

Fine art, photography, sculpture are all static art, available for up-close examination and scrutiny. Reading is fluid, but can slow down, speed up, or even go back. Film, and especially music are purely fluid arts, as in the *motion* picture arts. They are absorbed into our consciousnesses, experienced, in totally different ways.

I think 'challenging' films are actually extremely important in modern societies without many difficulties.  The advancement of civilization can be measured by how much suffering is removed from the lives of its members.  That suffering, however, is what motivated people to pursue critical thinking and take the actions which built our civilization.  It is very easy for people to become short-sighted.  For example, the anti-vaccination movement is populated with people who grew up ignorant of the ravages of the diseases vaccines prevent.  They have no visceral motivation to fear these diseases.  This makes it easy for them to convince one another that the diseases really aren't that bad, and that the risks attendant with vaccination, even though very small, are not worth taking.  You will not find people amongst anti-vaccination groups who grew up watching their classmates, friends, and family die or be crippled with preventable disease.  One dead child in their arms would be enough to convince them.

But, obviously, we can't go around letting children die simply to motivate people to vaccinate.  If we did this, we would be undoing civilization.  This is a Catch-22 type problem.  Remove the suffering, and you remove the visceral motivators.  Do not remove the suffering, and you fail to advance civilization.  I think that this is actually the single biggest problem that the human species faces.  As it becomes less and less necessary for a person to be reasonable in their thinking in order to be safe and comfortable, people engage in less critical thinking and come to believe that the infrastructure which keeps them safe is not worth the cost of its upkeep.  That threatens a collapse if that infrastructure is not maintained and improved.  And it would be a self-sustaining sort of collapse as well.  People would turn to the things people have always turned to throughout history - superstition and religion.  Those would support dismantling further the infrastructure of civilization.  

Watching films with content that causes the audience to step outside of their own situation and consider how things might be different is one of the things that can help prevent this.  Watching a film about the holocaust can encourage the consideration of questions like 'Why did so many people go along with it?'  Asking that question is the only chance we might ever have to make people insightful enough to avoid becoming a cog in a machine of genocide in the future.  

Why watch challenging movies?  Because they might save the world.

While everyone has their own tastes and their subjective take on whether a movie is "good" or "bad" is always valid, there are objective ways to measure the quality of a movie: whether it communicates its message effectively, whether it has elements that don't accomplish what they're supposed to or take the audience out of the moment or are simply distracting, whether the story flows properly and explains everything that needs explaining, etc. When using this more objective definition, I prefer the term "failed" movies, because that's what they are: movies that failed to communicate what they set out to communicate for whatever reasons.

With that in mind, there are lots of reasons to enjoy failed art. The most obvious is that they're often accidentally funny in their failure, because comedy that wasn't intended to be comedy is still entertaining to watch and because there's something satisfying about an artist swinging for the fences as hard as they can and coming nowhere near close to hitting the ball. There's also a lot of value in failed movies for people who understand and appreciate the mechanics of film as a medium and can benefit from seeing what happens when things are done incorrectly and asking what could be improved. Failed movies also tend to be daring, failing because they decided to try something really new and challenging instead of making a safe, derivative movie and it just didn't come together like they'd hoped, and those movies often have kernels of really interesting ideas that you just wouldn't find in any other movie and that you can see how they might have been great if certain decisions were made differently. And of course there is the appeal of kitsch, of liking something regardless of its "objective" quality just because you like it and you enjoy liking it and sharing that enjoyment with others who like it.

I guess the TL;DR is that failed movies often (I'd argue always) have *some* value as works of art, whether they're accidental comedy or a cautionary tale or an exploration of how the mechanics of film fail sometimes. I think that we should all strive to ask ourselves, when we see a film that is "bad", exactly why it is bad and maybe even why parts of it are good or enjoyable despite that. I know ever since I decided to do that, I've started liking all movies a lot more.
